name: Deodorant

lead: Deodorant gives you a cleaner, fresher scent, which matters because smell shapes how attractive you come across up close.

Underarm bacteria break down sweat, especially apocrine secretions that become active at puberty, and that produces odor. Deodorants mask it with fragrance, absorb moisture, or inhibit bacteria with ingredients such as alcohol, triclosan or alum. They do not reduce sweating; that is what antiperspirants do. In the US they are regulated as cosmetics.

paras: Applied to clean, dry underarms as a stick, spray or roll-on, usually daily and often layered with fragrance or alongside an antiperspirant. Odor control is noticeable straight away.
Some ingredients can cause skin irritation or contact dermatitis, and aerosols held too close can cause cold burns. Ingredients such as triclosan and phthalates have been studied for exposure.

angle.text: Deodorant controls underarm odor and adds scent, the basic step for smelling clean and being more pleasant to be near. The effect on odor is noticeable straight away.

lead: Deodorant is a product applied to the skin, most often the underarms, to prevent or mask body odor. Scent is part of how a person comes across in close contact, and looksmaxxing forums treat it as one more trait alongside grooming, skin and hair, with deodorant as the baseline layer before fragrance.[1][2] Deodorant works by masking smell with fragrance, by inhibiting the bacteria that turn sweat into odor, or by both; it does not stop sweating, which is the job of antiperspirants.[3][4]

The category includes sprays, roll-ons, sticks, gels, creams, wipes and crystal products made from potassium or ammonium alum, and many products combine deodorant and antiperspirant actives.[3][5] Underarm odor is produced when bacteria such as Corynebacterium, Staphylococcus and Propionibacterium break down compounds in apocrine sweat, and it is influenced by genetics, diet, sex and health.[1] Wikipedia dates the first modern commercial deodorant, Mum, to 1888 in Philadelphia.[3][6]

Published research on deodorants covers formulation and active agents, underarm microbiology, ingredient safety and skin reactions. No study has tested deodorant use against attractiveness ratings.[7][8][9]
infobox: Personal-care product (cosmetic in the US when it does not reduce sweat)[3]
Spray, roll-on, stick, gel, crystal alum, wipe[3][5]
Fragrance, alcohol, alum, antimicrobials; aluminium salts in antiperspirants[3][4]
Deodorants regulated as cosmetics; antiperspirant products as drugs[3][4]

paras: Formats include aerosol sprays and sticks, which Wikipedia describes as the two main types, as well as roll-ons, gels, creams, wipes and crystal products made from potassium or ammonium alum, a natural mineral salt that inhibits bacteria.[3][5] Whole-body deodorants exist as sprays, sticks, creams and wipes for use beyond the underarm.[3]

Active and supporting ingredients described in reference sources include alcohols and propylene glycol, which dry the skin and kill bacteria; antimicrobials such as triclosan, octenidine and parabens; methenamine; activated charcoal for absorbing sweat and odor; and fragrance or plant extracts for masking scent.[3] Antiperspirants add aluminium salts such as aluminium chlorohydrate, which react with sweat electrolytes to form gel plugs in sweat ducts and so reduce the moisture bacteria need.[3][4] A 2023 systematic review focused on newer alcohol-free, paraben-free and plant-derived agents and identified understanding gel-plug formation and achieving long-lasting benefit as the main challenges.[7] Natural options based on essential oils or plant extracts have grown in popularity since the 2010s.[5]
Some formulations use magnesium or zinc compounds rather than aluminium, and users have discussed magnesium oxide deodorants and their effect on skin bacteria on Hacker News.[10]

The benefit is olfactory rather than visual, but grooming guides and forum threads treat the two together. One looksmax.org poster who realised he had never used deodorant asked whether others notice it, and a reply argued that wearing fragrance makes people read you as richer, more confident and more sociable.[2] On T Nation, users associate the scent of particular deodorants such as Old Spice with masculinity.[11]

Forum users discuss deodorant as the first layer of scent grooming, applied before cologne or body spray; the wiki covers fragrance layering in separate entries. Underarm hair also plays a role, because hair wicks moisture away from the skin, which helps limit bacterial growth.[3]

Eccrine glands across much of the skin produce largely odorless sweat, while apocrine glands in the armpits and groin produce a thicker sweat with proteins, lipids and carbohydrates that bacteria metabolise.[3] Apocrine glands become active at puberty, which is why adult-type odor typically begins then.[3] Bacteria release volatile compounds, with Wikipedia naming trans-3-methyl-2-hexenoic acid as a primary source.[3]

Wikipedia states that Corynebacterium species break down sweat lipids into odorous molecules such as butyric acid, that Staphylococcus hominis produces thioalcohols, and that men and women tend to carry different bacterial populations, which the article links to different underarm smells.[1] The ABCC11 gene strongly influences underarm odor, and a common variant reduces secretion of odor precursors, most commonly in East Asian populations.[1] Washing with alkaline soap can disturb the skin acid mantle of about pH 4.5 to 6, which may make it easier for bacteria to colonise.[3]

Wikipedia credits Edna Murphey of Philadelphia with patenting Mum, the first modern commercial deodorant, in 1888; it was originally a zinc-based cream applied with the fingertips, and Bristol-Myers bought the small company in 1931.[3][6] The first commercial antiperspirant, Everdry, followed in 1903.[3] In 1941 Jules Montenier received a patent for an antiperspirant that combined aluminium chloride with a nitrile compound to reduce acidity and irritation, and it was used in the Stopette spray of the early 1950s.[3]

In the late 1940s Helen Barnett Diserens developed an applicator modelled on the ballpoint pen, and in 1952 it was marketed as Ban Roll-On; Mum Rollette followed in the UK and Commonwealth in 1958.[3][6] From 1942 to 1957 the deodorant market grew about 600 times, to roughly 70 million dollars, and expanded from women to men, with an estimated half of men using deodorants by 1957.[3]

Aerosols dominated from the early 1960s, when Gillette launched Right Guard, and by the early 1970s made up about 82 percent of US antiperspirant sales. In 1977 the FDA banned an aluminium zirconium aerosol ingredient over inhalation concerns, and limits on CFC propellants in the late 1970s shifted the market toward sticks.[3]

A 2015 study of 24 volunteers, with odor rated by four assessors, found that people who did not use antiperspirant had stronger underarm odor and many more bacteria than users; sequencing showed that Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium and Propionibacterium made up most sequences in non-users, and some groups differed between men and women and correlated with specific odor descriptors. A 2019 study examined how skin care products affect skin chemistry and microbiome dynamics.[8] A 2017 randomized trial reported effective axillary malodour reduction by deodorants containing polyquaternium-16.[12]

In the US, the FDA regulates deodorants as cosmetics and antiperspirants as drugs.[3][4] Possible reactions include irritation from propylene glycol, dermatitis from alum crystals, and allergic axillary reactions to fragrance components; experimental provocation studies have examined hydroxycitronellal and similar fragrance chemicals in deodorants for people with contact allergy.[3][9] Zirconium compounds have been linked to allergic granulomas in a 1976 report.[3] Aerosols held close to the skin can cause cold burns, with temperature drops of over 60 degrees Celsius measured in tests and a 2010 Pediatrics study documenting cases.[3]

Concerns about aluminium have circulated widely. The FDA concluded in 2003 that the data did not justify changing the status of aluminium antiperspirants; the EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety could not complete a risk assessment in 2015 because of limited absorption data and in 2020 judged aluminium compounds safe up to 6.25 percent in non-spray and 10.60 percent in spray products; a 2014 review of 469 studies found little evidence linking aluminium exposure to Alzheimer disease or cancer; and the US National Cancer Institute says studies on breast cancer have given conflicting results and that further research would be needed.[3][4] Wikipedia traces the breast cancer claim to a 1999 spam email and cites a 2008 review that found no risk.[3] The FDA advises people with kidney disease to consult a doctor before using aluminium-containing antiperspirants.[3]

Triclosan, a widely used antimicrobial, was reviewed in 1996 and measured in human plasma and milk in a 2006 Swedish study; fragrance-fixing phthalates in personal care products have been linked to urinary metabolite levels in women in a 2013 study; and a 2010 study linked frequent deodorant use with blood levels of the synthetic musk galaxolide.[13][14][15][3]

No studies found testing deodorant for attractiveness outcomes. Related research examines active agents and test methods, underarm microbiota, ingredient exposure and contact allergy.[7][8][13][14][15][12][9]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, deodorant and fragrance come up as part of scent as a trait, with users asking which products to use and whether skipping them matters.[16][17]
